title: Socrates and Plato
note: Socrates wrote nothing; he questioned Athenians about virtue and was executed in 399 BCE. His student Plato wrote dialogues, mostly with Socrates as speaker, and taught that eternal, unchanging Forms are the true objects of knowledge, while the changing things we see only participate in them.

read.title: The gadfly and the Forms
text: Socrates spent his life in the public places of Athens asking people what courage, piety, or justice is. When someone offered a definition, he drew out its consequences until the speaker contradicted himself. He said the oracle at Delphi had called him the wisest of men, and he concluded that his wisdom lay in recognizing his own ignorance. In 399 BCE a jury convicted him of impiety and corrupting the young, and he chose death over abandoning philosophy.

Plato, his student, turned these questions into a theory. If we can know what justice is, there must be something stable to know, yet every just act we see is partial and changing. Plato concluded that the true objects of knowledge are Forms, perfect and unchanging realities such as Justice itself and Beauty itself. Visible things participate in the Forms and so resemble them imperfectly.

In the Republic's Allegory of the Cave, prisoners take shadows on a wall for reality. A freed prisoner climbs out, sees real things in sunlight, and finally the sun itself, which stands for the Form of the Good. For Plato, education is this turning of the soul toward what is most real.
